blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: You see QR codes on menus, posters, and product labels. One small square can hold a website address, and your phone can read it even when it is tilted. How can black and white squares do this? And how can you check that a code is safe?

items.prompt: Where did you last see a QR code?
items.answer: Answers will vary. For example: I saw a QR code on a restaurant menu yesterday.

items.prompt: What do you usually do when you see a QR code?
items.answer: Answers will vary. For example: I open my phone camera and scan it.

items.prompt: What do you think a QR code can store?
items.answer: Answers will vary. For example: I think it stores a website address.

blocks.title: Part 1 — What Is a QR Code?
paragraphs: A QR code is a two-dimensional pattern of black and white squares. The letters QR stand for Quick Response. Unlike a barcode, which only stores information in one direction (left to right), a QR code stores information in two directions — across and down. This means it can hold much more data in a small space. For example, a single QR code can store a full website address, a phone number, or even a short message.

blocks.title: Check — What Is a QR Code?

items.prompt: How is a QR code different from a barcode?
items.answer: A QR code stores information in two directions — across and down — so it can hold more data than a barcode, which only stores information in one direction.

blocks.title: Part 2 — Modules and Size
paragraphs: The small black and white squares inside a QR code are called modules. Every module is either black or white, and together they form a code. A simple QR code — for example, one that stores just a short word — needs fewer modules and is smaller. A complex QR code — for example, one that stores a long web address — needs more modules and becomes larger. The more data you put in, the bigger the code gets.

images.alt: A small simple QR pattern points to a larger, denser pattern that can hold more data.

items.prompt: Why does a QR code get bigger when it stores more data?
items.answer: Because more data needs more modules. A larger QR code contains more black and white squares to hold all the extra information.

blocks.title: Part 3 — How Your Phone Reads a QR Code
paragraphs: Look at a QR code and you will notice three square shapes in three corners. These are called position patterns. They help your phone's camera find the code and understand which direction it is facing — even if the code is upside down or tilted. Once the camera locates the three corner squares, it reads the modules across and down and turns the pattern into data. This is why scanning is so fast: the position patterns act like a map.

images.alt: A phone camera uses the three highlighted corner squares to find a QR code direction.

items.prompt: What do the three corner squares in a QR code do?
items.answer: They are position patterns. They help the camera find the code and know which direction it is facing, making scanning fast even if the code is tilted or upside down.

blocks.title: Part 4 — What Happens When a QR Code Is Damaged?
paragraphs: A QR code has a built-in safety feature called error correction. This means that even if part of the code is dirty, torn, or covered, some missing data can still be restored and read correctly. The code stores extra information that helps rebuild some missing pieces automatically. This is why a QR code may still work when a small part is hard to see.

items.prompt: Why can a QR code still work when part of it is covered by a logo?
items.answer: Because QR codes have error correction. The code stores extra copies of the data, so missing or covered parts can be rebuilt and read correctly.

blocks.title: Part 5 — Staying Safe When You Scan
paragraphs: QR codes are useful, but they can also open harmful or fake websites. Scammers may use a QR code to send you to a page that tries to steal your personal information. Before you open a link, always check the web address on your screen. If the address looks strange, the code is unexpected, or it pressures you to act quickly, do not open it.

images.alt: A learner pauses to check a web address and warning sign before opening a QR code link.

items.prompt: What should you do before you open a link from a QR code?
items.answer: You should check the web address on your screen first. If it looks strange or the code is asking you to act quickly, do not open the link.

items.prompt: You are at a café and you see a QR code on the table for the menu. What do you do before you open the link, and why?
items.answer: I scan the code, then I look at the web address on my screen. If the address looks correct and normal, I open it. I do this because a fake QR code sticker could send me to a harmful website.
